{{short description|Italian philosopher}}
[[File:Pacius.png|thumb|Giulio Pace]]

'''Giulio Pace de Beriga''', also known as '''Giulio Pacio''', or by his Latin name '''Julius Pacius of Beriga''' (9 April 1550 – 1635) was a well-known Italian [[Aristotle|Aristotelian]] scholar and jurist.

==Life==
He was born in [[Vicenza]], [[Italy]], and studied [[law]] and [[philosophy]] in [[University of Padua|Padua]].

He was deeply moved by the [[Protestant Reformation|Reformation]]. The [[Catholic Church]] considered him immoral and a lover of [[heresy|heretical]] writings and he found himself put on [[Trial (law)|trial]] by the [[Inquisition]]. Fleeing first to [[Geneva]] to escape their wrath, he soon converted to [[Protestantism]] while in [[Heidelberg]].

His academic career was wide and varied, as he became an itinerant figure. In Geneva, he was elected as a public professor, and taught from 1575 to 1585. Studious and having a deep knowledge of [[Greek language|Greek]], he translated Aristotle. He taught law at the [[University of Heidelberg]], from 1585 to 1594. Incidentally, while he was at Heidelberg, his quarrels with compatriot [[Scipione Gentili]] ultimately compelled the latter to leave for [[University of Altdorf|Altdorf]]. Also while there he showed his [[Ramist]] sympathies, but came into conflict with the philosophical faculty for trying to give private tuition in Ramist logic.<ref>http://fds.oup.com/www.oup.co.uk/pdf/0-19-817430-6.pdf {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110521092610/http://fds.oup.com/www.oup.co.uk/pdf/0-19-817430-6.pdf |date=2011-05-21 }}, p. 22.</ref> After spending 1595 teaching logic at the [[Academy of Sedan]], he was [[Provost (education)|provost]] and prefect of studies at the [[University of Nimes]], from 1597 to 1600. He also taught philosophy in [[Hungary]], [[Leiden]] in the [[Netherlands]], [[Grenoble]] in [[France]], and in other places.{{Citation needed|date=December 2008}} At the [[University of Montpellier]], where he was from 1600 to 1616, [[Nicolas Claude Fabri de Peiresc]] was his pupil.<ref>[http://galileo.rice.edu/Catalog/NewFiles/peiresc.html Galileo Project page]</ref> He also taught at the [[University of Valence]], 1620-1, before taking a position at Padua where he taught from 1621 to 1635.<ref>Charles B. Schmitt, Quentin Skinner (editors), ''The Cambridge History of Renaissance Philosophy'' (1990), pp. 828-9.</ref>

==Works==
[[File:Pace, Giulio – De dominio maris Hadriatici, 1619 – BEIC 13725163.jpg|thumb|''De dominio maris Hadriatici'', 1619]]

Pace's edition of the ''[[Organon]]'' became standard during its life of 11 editions between 1584 and 1623, and even longer in the north of Europe. He also wrote a great many legal titles.

Pace wrote a pocket summary of [[Ramon Llull]]'s art, first in [[Latin]] in 1618 and then in [[French language|French]] in 1619. This work is seen as exceptional among its contemporaries as it does not digress into [[alchemy]], [[Christian Kabbalah|cabalism]], or [[Magic (paranormal)|magic]], and in fact stays true to Llull's traditional interests. Pace wrote a similar work for [[Petrus Ramus|Ramus]] as well.

Despite being a Protestant, in 1619, he published "De dominio maris Hadriatici dissertatio", defending the claims of the [[Venetian Republic]] to dominion over the [[Adriatic Sea]], against the opposite claims of the Empire and the [[Kingdom of Naples]]. This controversy in early international law lined him up with [[Paolo Sarpi]], against [[Juan Bautista Valenzuela Velázquez]] and Lorenzo Motino.<ref>Guido Acquaviva, ''Il Dominio di Venezia sul Mare Adriatico nelle opere di Paolo Sarpi e Giulio Pace'' (Giuffre': Milan, 2007) ({{ISBN|88-14-13440-5}}</ref><ref>Jan Hendrik Willem Verzijl, Wybo P. Heere, J. P. S. Offerhaus, ''International Law in Historical Perspective: Nationality and other matters relating to individuals'' (1968), p. 14.</ref>

A book was written on the life of Giulio Pace in the early 20th century, focusing on his work as a jurist.<ref>Antonio Franceschini, ''Giulio Pace da Beriga e la giurisprudenza dei suoi tempi'', Venezia: Officine Grafiche di Carlo Ferrari, 1903,</ref>
